transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-03-11 15:30 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Samir Rao (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Gale - Head of ML), Marcus Lee (Gale - Platform), Dana Ortiz (Gale - CTO)
Recording: Auto-generated transcript (medium quality)

Summary (auto): Explore cost and deployment options; prioritize predictability and data residency; run benchmarks.

[00:00] Jordan Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'm Jordan, AE on the Redwood Inference team. Samir and I will walk through options — quick run of who you are?
[00:07] Priya Nair: Hi, Priya here. I run ML at Gale, mostly focused on RAG and summarization for our customer service product.
[00:12] Marcus Lee: Marcus, platform infra, responsible for deployments, networking, and cost ops.
[00:15] Dana Ortiz: Dana, CTO, listening for budget and risk alignment.
[00:18] Samir Rao: Samir, SE at Redwood, I look after performance and Dedicated/Private onboarding.
[00:22] Jordan: Cool. Priya, can you give a quick sense of target latency, request shape, and budget constraints?
[00:30] Priya: Yeah so our typical user query is about 120 tokens on average, sometimes longer with retrieval up to 1k tokens. Peak qps around 60, sustained 20, and we have a hard budget cap — across all inference spend we want to stay under $45k per month to start. We're evaluating hosted for speed vs Dedicated for predictable cost. Also some customers ask for data residency in EU, so private is on the table.
[00:50] Jordan: Great, that's the profile we needed. Two quick framing points: hosted gives fastest time-to-value and predictable per-token billing but can spike; Dedicated gives reserved GPU capacity so throughput/lower per-token cost with commit; Private gives control for residency and keys but higher ops. We'll talk about levers — batching, caching (prefix/KV cache), quantization — and how they move the per-token cost.
[01:18] Marcus: When you say per-token, can you ballpark numbers? We just need a sanity check to see if $45k/mo is feasible for our load.
[01:25] Samir: Sure, very rough: hosted generation might be around $0.0014 to $0.0028 per generated token depending on model and seq length — these are example ranges. Dedicated reserved capacity modeling often brings that down by 40-70% at scale, depending on utilization and batching. With aggressive batching and prefix/KV cache for repeated assistant prompts, you can get another 10-35% savings. Quantization (int8/int4 on some models) can reduce GPU costs further but it depends on model compatibility and latency SLOs.
[02:05] Dana: Those are helpful. I know numbers vary per model — are you able to run our sample prompts to produce a model-specific unit econ?
[02:12] Samir: Absolutely — that's what the Dedicated benchmark is for. We'll run your prompt set across a couple of candidate models and give you per-token time and estimated cost under hosted vs Dedicated commit scenarios.
[02:22] Priya: One nuance — many of our calls are RAG so there's an embed step per doc and then a generation. Any thoughts on embedding cost and caching?
[02:30] Jordan: Yes, embedding is typically charged per-embedding unit; you can amortize embeddings with caching on the app side. On Redwood we also support embedding caches for repeated doc retrievals. Seems like in your pattern we can model embedding cost separately and likely it's a small fraction of the monthly spend if you cache frequently accessed knowledge.
[02:53] Marcus: Ok, about batching — our traffic has spikes. If we rely on batching for lower unit cost, will that increase latency and create unhappy users?
[02:59] Samir: There's always a tradeoff. Continuous batching in the runtime tries to pack requests within tight latency windows to reduce per-token compute. For example, if you allow 25-50ms extra scheduling latency, batch sizes can jump and reduce per-token compute by ~20-40%. For very latency-sensitive paths (sub-200ms end-to-end) we recommend a hybrid: low-latency hosted instances for critical calls and Dedicated/batched for non-interactive or background tasks.
[03:35] Priya: We're also evaluating a plan to serve top-tier customers with private deployment due to residency and contractual terms. How mature is the Private offering for on-prem or VPC?
[03:43] Jordan: Private is mature for VPC-based deployments; on-prem air-gap packages exist but the path is heavier. Private gives you KMS/HSM integration, RBAC, audit logs, and a customer-managed control plane option. We'll send the security pack.
[03:58] Marcus: Speaking of KMS, does Redwood integrate with our cloud provider KMS and can keys be customer-managed?
[04:05] Samir: Yes — for Private we support customer-managed keys via standard KMS APIs; for Hosted we offer envelope encryption with Redwood-managed keys or customer BYOK for enterprise contracts. We'll include the exact integration docs in the security packet.
[04:20] Dana: Good. On SLOs — we're sensitive to timeouts. If you fall back to a smaller model to preserve latency, does Redwood provide automatic fallback?
[04:28] Jordan: Yes, smart routing can fallback to compatible model variants automatically by policy. You can configure region, cost, and latency preferences per route. We also support canary rollouts so you can test a replacement model gradually.
[04:42] Priya: Back to per-token — can you show an example model of how batching and caching change the monthly bill? A toy calc is fine.
[04:49] Samir: Sure, quick toy calc on the call: assume 20 sustained qps, average 120 tokens generated per request, that's 20*120*3600*24*30 approx. but let's do simpler: 20 rps * 120 tokens = 2400 tokens/sec -> ~207M tokens/day -> ~6.2B tokens/month. At hosted rate of $0.0015 per token generated, that's $9.3M — OK that's unrealistic for you because we double counted something, sorry — let me re-run — ah, math slip, yes, too big because 20 rps continuous is a lot. For your stated workload earlier (sustained 20 qps but likely lower effective usage per user and caching) we expect monthly tokens in the low hundreds of millions range, not billions. The important takeaway is small changes in per-token have big dollar effects.
[06:00] Marcus: We're glad you caught that. Can you instead model target: stay under $45k/mo with our expected traffic profile?
[06:07] Samir: Yes. Rough approach: run your actual prompt set in the benchmark to get per-call token counts and latency; apply hosted and Dedicated unit costs. With Dedicated we can propose a reserved capacity tier that targets your peaks and leaves some burst; the committed monthly commitment is often a fixed amount that makes sense for your budget. We'll show three scenarios: 1) Hosted only; 2) Dedicated + Hosted hybrid; 3) Private (capex + ops) estimate.
[06:34] Priya: For scenario 2 (hybrid), what percent of traffic would you recommend sending to Dedicated to hit our budget?
[06:40] Samir: Typical pattern: send 60-80% of non-latency-critical traffic to Dedicated. For example, background generation, batch summarization, and mid-tier customers go to Dedicated. Latency-critical interactive edges remain on hosted. That mix often reduces unit cost enough that overall bill hits enterprise budgets. Exact number depends on your cache hit rate and batching windows. If your cache hit is 30% and batching yields 35% saving on remaining, that compounds.
[07:06] Marcus: What about prefix caching — in our RAG flow the prompt shares a large system prompt repeated across calls. How easy is it to cache the KV/ prefix and how much savings?
[07:14] Samir: Prefix/KV cache stores the tokenized representation so you don't recompute the prefix on every call, and you avoid processing those tokens on the GPU each time. Gains depend on how many tokens are repeated — if the repeated prefix is 200 tokens out of 400 total, you can save roughly 40-60% of compute for that segment. In practice we see 15-35% effective per-token cost reductions for RAG apps with high prefix reuse.
[07:41] Priya: Any limitations on cache consistency with dynamic context?
[07:44] Samir: If your prefix changes per user, caching helps less. We support multi-tenant keys and TTLs for cache entries — you can tune invalidation. We'll capture specifics in the benchmark design.
[07:55] [00:08:00] Jordan: Quick pause — Marcus, any procurement constraints on committed monthly spend or approval cycles?
[08:03] Marcus: Procurement requires a PO for anything above $50k per month, and the finance team wants to see predictable burn. If Dedicated gets us under that threshold we might prefer it.
[08:14] Dana: Our security team will also insist on SOC2 and audit logs for Private or Dedicated, right?
[08:19] Jordan: Yes, Dedicated customers get access to more detailed audit logs and can request extended retention as an add-on. Private offers full control over logs. We'll share the SOC2 summary and log retention options.
[08:31] Priya: Are there hidden costs — e.g., data egress, storage for embeddings, or per-request metadata?
[08:36] Samir: Good question. Embedding storage is typically billed separately if you use Redwood's managed index store; otherwise you manage it. Data egress depends on deployment (VPC/private reduces vendor egress). We'll list line items in the pricing sheet so nothing is hidden.
[08:50] Marcus: For benchmarking, what do you need from us?
[08:52] Samir: Your representative prompt set, distribution of request sizes, target SLOs (p50/p95 latency), and sample documents for RAG. Also indicate any models you prefer (open models vs Llama-derived vs others).
[09:04] Priya: We'll share those. One more practical point — our infra team is worried about warmup and cold starts increasing tail latency. How do you handle warmup?
[09:12] Samir: Runtime keeps warm pools for Dedicated. For Hosted, we provide options to keep pre-warmed replicas for critical routes at a small additional cost. Also, KV cache and prefix caching reduce cold computation.
[09:25] [00:12:00] Jordan: Let's talk about an example scoped pilot: 2-week Dedicated benchmark using your prompt set across two model sizes. We'll measure throughput, latency, and per-token costs, and produce a committed capacity recommendation. Cost for the benchmark itself is usually credited if you sign a Dedicated commitment. Does that sound reasonable?
[09:43] Marcus: Yes, finance and procurement will need an estimate up front.
[09:48] Dana: Also, can we simulate worst-case peak for Black Friday style loads?
[09:52] Samir: Absolutely — we can run burst tests and show autoscaling behaviors and fallbacks. We'll demonstrate graceful degradation with smaller models and routing policies.
[09:59] Priya: Any options for mixed-precision or quantized variants to save cost without impacting accuracy much?
[10:04] Samir: Yes, quantization (INT8, INT4) is a big lever. Some models maintain quality with int8; int4 sometimes introduces quality regressions depending on tasks. Our Optimize toolkit suggests quantization profiles per model and workload. We'll include model-specific guidance after the benchmark.
[10:20] Marcus: What's the onboarding timeline for Dedicated + Private if we wanted to pursue both?
[10:25] Jordan: Typical Dedicated onboarding is weeks: contract, capacity planning, and a 2-week benchmark. Private (VPC) is 4-8 weeks depending on networking and compliance checks. On-prem longer.
[10:36] Dana: Given our vendor approval timeline, we'll likely need procurement and security reviews in parallel.
[10:40] Jordan: We can coordinate with your procurement and security folks — we often provide SOC2 docs, security questionnaires, and a design review.
[10:48] [00:16:00] Priya: Quick objection — if we keep everything hosted to avoid ops, will we lose the cost predictability we need?
[10:56] Samir: Hosted is predictable per-token but total cost can vary with usage. Dedicated gives predictability by locking in capacity. The hybrid approach is a common compromise to keep ops low while hitting budget targets.
[11:08] Marcus: Another concern: our legal team wants clear data retention and deletion guarantees. Does Redwood provide deletion APIs and audit trails?
[11:15] Jordan: Yes, data deletion APIs are available and audit trails can be surfaced. For Private, you control retention. We'll attach the deletion flow in the security packet.
[11:26] [00:20:00] Samir: Let's capture the benchmark plan now: 1) Receive prompt set and traffic profile; 2) Redwood runs two candidate models on Dedicated with your sample traffic for 2 weeks; 3) We report p50/p95 latencies, throughput, cache hit rates, and per-token compute cost; 4) We produce three pricing scenarios.
[11:50] Priya: Sounds good. Any tips to increase batching effectiveness without hurting UX?
[11:55] Samir: If you can accept 20-50ms additional scheduling delay but keep network RTT low, batching usually wins. Also group non-interactive requests and prioritize routing. Use longer-lived sessions for multi-turn chats to increase KV cache reuse.
[12:09] Marcus: Regarding pricing model variants — do you offer reserved capacity with flexible burst credits?
[12:14] Jordan: Yes, Dedicated reservations include configurable burst pools and autoscaling policies. We can model different commit levels and show how burst credits reduce peak overprovisioning.
[12:24] [00:24:00] Dana: Are there examples of customers who've transitioned from hosted to hybrid and seen concrete savings?
[12:30] Jordan: Yes, we have case studies — we'll send a two-pager. One retail customer reduced per-token cost by ~55% after moving stable workloads to Dedicated and enabling prefix caching.
[12:40] Priya: Great. Anything else we should consider?
[12:43] Samir: Consider observability — token-level cost breakdowns, model-level latency dashboards, and regression alerts. Redwood Console ties these to prompts for quality monitoring. That helps prevent regressions when you quantize or change batching windows.
[12:59] Marcus: That helps procurement — being able to show expected ROI.
[13:03] [00:28:00] Jordan: Ok recap and owners: Jordan will send the pricing spreadsheet and security packet; Samir will set up the Dedicated benchmark slot and test harness; Priya will share prompt set and traffic profile. We'll reconvene after benchmark scheduling.
[13:18] Priya: We'll aim to get materials over by 2028-03-15.
[13:22] Jordan: Great. Any final questions?
[13:25] Dana: One last thing — SLA expectations on Dedicated?
[13:29] Samir: Dedicated comes with an SLA for uptime and latency targets depending on commit level; we'll include SLA terms in the proposal.
[13:36] Marcus: Thanks all, appreciate the concretes.
[13:38] [00:32:00] Jordan: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the documents and schedule.
[13:41] [laughter]
[13:45] Meeting end.
